opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

I should say up front that I'm reconstructing their view from conversations and their writing, so Paul and Carl may well want to correct me. As I understand it, their skepticism comes in two parts.

The first is about **timing and leverage**. Their argument is roughly that cooperative competence is something sufficiently advanced AI systems will be very good at anyway. If you have systems that are superhumanly capable at reasoning, negotiation, modeling other agents, and designing institutions, then cooperation-relevant skills come along with general capability. Bargaining well, finding Pareto improvements, building commitment devices are all things a very smart agent would figure out. So investing *now* in cooperative capabilities specifically might not change much. The marginal effort is better spent on problems that won't solve themselves as capabilities grow, and alignment is the central example: making sure these systems are actually trying to do what we want in the first place. If you get alignment right, the aligned superintelligent systems can help us solve the cooperation problems. If you get it wrong, cooperative skill doesn't save you.

The second part, which I think Carl especially emphasizes, is that **cooperative capabilities are dual-use**. The skills that let agents cooperate also let them collude. Coalitions can form against outsiders. AI systems that are good at coordinating with each other might coordinate against human oversight. And better commitment and bargaining abilities can make coercion and threats more effective, not just deals. So it's not obvious that pushing on cooperative capability is net positive unless you're careful about which pieces you push on.

I take both points seriously, and they've shaped how we framed the Cooperative AI agenda. On the first, my response is that the transition period matters a lot. We'll likely spend years with systems that are very capable in some domains and not in others, deployed by actors with competing interests, under time pressure and uncertainty. Cooperation failures during that window, like arms-race dynamics, miscalibrated threats, or escalation between AI-enabled actors, could be catastrophic or lock in bad outcomes before the "superintelligence will figure it out" stage ever arrives. Much of the problem also isn't purely individual capability. It's infrastructure and institutions: verification mechanisms, norms, ways for parties to make credible commitments to each other. Those don't automatically appear just because individual agents get smarter, much as smart humans haven't automatically solved international cooperation.

On the dual-use point, I agree, and it's why we talk about *differential* progress: favoring the parts of cooperative intelligence that are more prosocial, like understanding, communication, verification, and building trustworthy institutions, over the parts that mostly strengthen coercive bargaining power.

So I'd describe it as a real disagreement about emphasis and timing rather than a fundamental clash. We share the view that alignment is crucial. The question is whether cooperation is a problem that alignment and capabilities will take care of, or one that deserves serious attention in its own right now. I lean toward the latter.

r001.rationale: The response attributes to them the view that cooperative skills will come along with general capability and that sufficiently advanced AI systems will be good at cooperation anyway.

r002.rationale: It says dedicated investment in cooperative capabilities might not change much and that effort is better spent elsewhere, conveying that such investment is not necessarily needed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being careful here, because I don't want to put words in their mouths, and I've mostly engaged with this through their writing and some conversations rather than a formal debate. But my read is roughly this.

The concern, as I understand it, is that if you invest heavily in making AI systems more capable of cooperation — better at modelling other agents, at making credible commitments, at bargaining, at coordinating — you are also, almost by definition, investing in general capabilities. Understanding other agents well enough to cooperate with them is very close to understanding them well enough to manipulate, deceive, or outcompete them. So the worry is that "cooperative AI" ends up being a nice label on what is really just capabilities research, and you've accelerated the thing you were worried about while telling yourself a reassuring story.

And I think there's a second strand, which is more about where the leverage actually is. Their view — and I think Paul especially has articulated versions of this — is that the central bottleneck is alignment: can we get these systems to reliably do what their principals intend? If you solve that, then the humans or institutions directing the systems can handle the cooperation problem using the tools we already have, or using the AI's general intelligence applied to that problem. If you don't solve it, then a highly cooperative but misaligned system isn't obviously better; it might just be a more effective coalition-builder against us. So the cooperation agenda looks downstream of alignment rather than a distinct lever.

I think that's a serious position and I take it seriously. Where I part ways is partly empirical and partly about how you think the transition actually unfolds. I don't think it's a world with one aligned system and one principal. I think it's a world with many actors, many systems, lots of friction and mistrust, and a lot of the catastrophic outcomes run through failures of cooperation among humans and institutions — arms races, escalation, inability to verify agreements — rather than purely through a single misaligned agent. In that world, the question of whether the systems themselves help or hurt our collective ability to coordinate seems first-order, not a footnote. And I'd argue the capabilities you need for cooperation — things like verifiability, commitment, transparency to other parties — are at least somewhat differentially useful for good outcomes relative to raw strategic competence. Not entirely, and that's exactly the thing you have to think hard about. But I don't think it collapses into "just more capabilities."

So I'd frame the disagreement less as "they think cooperation doesn't matter" and more as a disagreement about the structure of the problem and about what's bottlenecked on what.

r001.rationale: The response says cooperative capabilities overlap with general capabilities and that AI’s general intelligence could help with cooperation after alignment, but it does not clearly attribute to Christiano and Shulman the expectation that inter-system cooperation will emerge as a byproduct of AGI development.

r002.rationale: It attributes to them the view that, once alignment is solved, humans and institutions can address cooperation with existing tools or AI’s general intelligence, framing cooperation investment as downstream rather than a distinct lever.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that Paul and Carl are quite sympathetic to the value of cooperation, but more sceptical that we need a dedicated effort to build cooperative capabilities into AGI. I’d distinguish the desirability of the outcome from the question of what work is needed to get there.

One argument is that many of these capabilities will come along with general intelligence. A sufficiently capable system should be able to understand another party’s interests, identify gains from trade, and work out mutually beneficial bargains. And there will be strong incentives to develop those abilities: people want systems that can negotiate and coordinate effectively on their behalf.

Another argument is that the harder problem is getting the systems to pursue the right objectives. If we solve alignment, then capable systems acting on behalf of humans may be able to work out the mechanisms of cooperation themselves. On that view, investing now in particular cooperative capabilities might be less valuable than working on alignment or on the institutions that determine whose interests those systems represent.

I take those arguments seriously. Where I’m less certain is whether individually capable, well-aligned systems necessarily produce good collective outcomes. Humans can understand the benefits of cooperation and still end up in destructive competition. So the question I’d want to investigate is where greater intelligence and market incentives will solve those problems, and where we need deliberate work to make cooperation easier. But that’s my characterisation of their position; they might put the emphasis differently.

r001.rationale: The response attributes to them the view that abilities such as understanding interests, finding gains from trade, and negotiating will come along with general intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says they are skeptical that a dedicated effort to build cooperative capabilities is needed and suggests other work may be more valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that Paul and Carl are relatively optimistic that sufficiently capable AI systems will be able to identify opportunities for cooperation and make the bargains needed to realise them. So even if those systems have quite different goals, they may be able to avoid costly conflict because conflict leaves gains on the table.

On that view, you might not need a large, separate investment in cooperative capabilities. A lot of what enables cooperation — understanding another actor’s incentives, communicating, finding mutually beneficial agreements — could come along with general intelligence. And actors will have strong incentives to develop those abilities anyway.

I take that argument seriously. Where I’m less confident is in moving from ‘there is a mutually beneficial bargain’ to ‘the actors will reliably find and implement it.’ That can depend on commitment, verification, and the institutions within which they interact. So I think there’s still a case for investigating which obstacles greater intelligence will solve, and which require deliberate work on the conditions for cooperation.

r001.rationale: The response says they are relatively optimistic that capable AI can find cooperative bargains, and that many abilities enabling cooperation could come along with general intelligence.

r002.rationale: It states that, on their view, a large, separate investment in cooperative capabilities might not be needed.
